newsitem.title: UK: A year on, London little troubled by bomb fallout.
newsitem.headline: A year on, London little troubled by bomb fallout.

text.p: A year after the Irish Republican Army ended its ceasefire and devastated London's showcase Docklands business district, there are few lingering effects on the everyday life of the capital.

Smashed windows can still be seen in the high-rises that felt the blast of the bomb last February 9, killing two and injuring 100. Rebuilding at east London's Canary Wharf is described by local authorities as "a lengthy process".
But elsewhere in the capital the shadow of the bomber can hardly be said to be troubling a booming city that style pundits have dubbed "the coolest place on the planet".

A decision to close Hammersmith bridge over the Thames in west London for routine repairs that could take two years has caused more complaints and disruption than when the IRA set off a bomb there last April.

The number of tourists visiting London rose strongly last year to an estimated 25.1 million, despite the end of the IRA's truce, and is forecast to rise by another million this year despite renewed guerrilla violence in recent weeks.

Even Americans, fearful of crossing the Atlantic during the Gulf crisis in 1990 and 1991, now seem to disregard the prospect of bomb attacks in London, perhaps because the United States has in recent years begun to suffer such attacks at home.
"We didn't notice any long-term decline in people coming to London because of that decision by the IRA," said Christine Shaw of the London Tourist Board.
"There was a slight dip after the Docklands bomb, but it picked up immediately."
She added: "Americans have had their own domestic experience of bombings. Perhaps it has become more familiar to them and they realise that life goes on for most people after a bomb explosion."
And if there was going to be more violence, as security sources have suggested, maybe London is no bad place to be.
"We've had experience of dealing with terrorism over a long period," said Shaw. "We know how to protect people."
The shock of the Canary Wharf attack was closely followed by an "own-goal" explosion on a double-decker bus in which a bomber died, apparently on his way to plant another London bomb.

Since then there have been three minor bomb attacks and a number of seizures of bomb-making materials, but Londoners have mostly had to deal with the small change of the IRA's resumed bombing campaign.
Streets and stations are often cordoned off while bomb squad experts are called in to deal with "suspect packages." Usually, someone's forgotten a bag of shopping.
London's financial district, hit by two massive bombs in 1992 and 1993, had already taken its own measures against further attacks.

A security cordon of traffic barriers and security cameras dubbed the "ring of plastic" was set up in 1993 to enable police to check vehicles entering the "square mile" after foreign banks demanded action to protect them against the bombers.
Even though it was extended slightly last month to provide what local authorities called "a more secure environment", it too, has become a barely noticed fact of life for busy Londoners.

It has had side effects the bombers can hardly have dreamed of. Within its perimeter, traffic has eased, air pollution has declined, recorded crime is down by a third and road accidents have fallen by 40 percent.
